Authors: Tuchscherer, Rhianna M, Thompson, Angela M, Trujillo, Jennifer M | Year: 2018 | Journal: The Annals of pharmacotherapy
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To review efficacy and safety of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) semaglutide for type 2 diabetes (T2D).
DATA SOURCES
A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and EMBASE using the term semaglutide was completed through April 2018. A search of clinicaltrials.gov was also conducted.
STUDY SELECTION AND DATA EXTRACTION
English-language studies assessing the efficacy and/or safety of semaglutide were evaluated.

Semaglutide is a newly approved GLP-1 RA for the treatment of T2D. Administered once weekly at a dose of 0.5 or 1 mg, it has been compared with placebo, sitagliptin, insulin glargine, a combination of oral antidiabetic therapies, and 2 GLP-1 RAs, exenatide ER and dulaglutide, and demonstrated greater efficacy compared with these therapies. <snippet id="34697882">Title: A model-based simulation of glycaemic control and body weight when switching from semaglutide to 3.0- and 4.5-mg doses of once-weekly dulaglutide.
Authors: Tham, Lai San, Pantalone, Kevin M, Dungan, Kathleen et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Diabetes, obesity & metabolism
Abstract: AIM
To evaluate HbA1c and body weight changes when semaglutide 0.5- or 1.0-mg once-weekly (QW) is switched to dulaglutide 3.0- or 4.5-mg QW via exposure-response modelling.
METHODS
HbA1c and body weight time-course models were developed and validated with data from the SUSTAIN 1 to 10 trials for semaglutide and the AWARD-11 trial for dulaglutide. Simulations were conducted for HbA1c and body weight over 52 weeks. In the initial 26 weeks, semaglutide was initiated at 0.25-mg and titrated to 0.5- or 1.0-mg QW via 4-weekly stepwise titration, followed by 26 weeks of dulaglutide initiated at 0.75- or 1.5-mg QW and escalated to 3.0- or 4.5-mg QW via 4-weekly stepwise titration.
RESULTS
At 26 weeks, model-predicted mean changes from baseline in HbA1c and weight for semaglutide 0.5 mg were up to -1.55% and -3.44 kg, respectively. After switching to dulaglutide 3.0 mg, further reductions were 0.19% and 1.40 kg, respectively, at 52 weeks. Predicted mean HbA1c and weight changes for semaglutide 1.0 mg at 26 weeks were -1.84% and -4.96 kg, respectively; after switching to dulaglutide 4.5 mg, HbA1c was maintained with additional weight reduction of up to 0.57 kg at 52 weeks. Glycaemic control was preserved when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 mg.
CONCLUSION
Switching from semaglutide 0.5 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 or 4.5 mg with dose escalation potentially yields additional HbA1c and weight reductions; switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 4.5 mg may enhance weight loss.</snippet>

<snippet id="29574633">Title: A Network Meta-Analysis Comparing Semaglutide Once-Weekly with Other GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Japanese Patients with Type 2 Diabetes.
Authors: Webb, Neil, Orme, Michelle, Witkowski, Michal et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Diabetes therapy : research, treatment and education of diabetes and related disorders
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Semaglutide once-weekly (QW) is a novel glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) analogue administered at a 0.5 or 1.0 mg dose. In the absence of head-to-head trials between semaglutide QW and other GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) in a Japanese population, a network meta-analysis (NMA) was performed. The objective was to assess the relative efficacy and safety of semaglutide QW vs GLP-1 RAs in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM), with a specific focus on the comparison between semaglutide 0.5 mg QW and dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW.
METHODS
A systematic review (SR) and supplementary Japanese searches were conducted to identify trials of GLP-1 RAs in Japanese patients on diet and exercise, who have previously received 0-1 oral antidiabetic drugs (OADs). Data at 52-56 weeks were extracted for the following outcomes (feasible for analysis in an NMA): glycated hemoglobin (HbA 1c ), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), weight, systolic blood pressure (SBP), and overall hypoglycemia. The data were synthesized using an NMA and a Bayesian framework.
RESULTS
Four trials, identified from the SR and Japanese-specific searches, were relevant for inclusion in the NMA. When compared to dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW, semaglutide 0.5 mg QW was shown to provide significant reductions in HbA 1c [- 0.61% (12.3 mmol/mol)], weight (- 1.45 kg), SBP (- 5.03 mmHg), and FPG (- 1.26 mmol/L). No significant differences in the proportion of patients achieving a HbA 1c level < 7% (53 mmol/mol) or the risk of overall hypoglycemia were observed between semaglutide 0.5 mg QW and dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW.
CONCLUSION
Overall, semaglutide 0.5 mg QW was associated with significant reductions from baseline in HbA 1c , weight, SBP, and FPG compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW in Japanese patients with T2DM. These data may provide valuable evidence for clinical decision-making, cost-effectiveness analyses, and health technology appraisal (HTA) requirements.
FUNDING
Novo Nordisk Pharma Ltd.</snippet>
<snippet id="34622548">Title: Efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide by baseline age in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes: A subgroup analysis of the PIONEER 9 and 10 Japan trials.
Authors: Yamada, Yuichiro, Yabe, Daisuke, Hertz, Christin Løth et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Diabetes, obesity & metabolism
Abstract: A post-hoc exploratory analysis of the PIONEER 9 and 10 trials evaluated the effect of baseline age (<65 and ≥65 years) on the efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes. In PIONEER 9 and 10, patients were randomized to once-daily oral semaglutide (3, 7 or 14 mg) or a comparator (placebo or once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide 0.9 mg [PIONEER 9]; once-weekly subcutaneous dulaglutide 0.75 mg [PIONEER 10]) for 52 weeks, with 5 weeks' follow-up. In total, 701 patients were included (PIONEER 9: N = 243; PIONEER 10: N = 458). Glycaemic efficacy of oral semaglutide was similar in Japanese patients aged <65 years compared with those ≥65 years, and there did not appear to be a clear pattern between age subgroup and body weight changes. Across treatment arms, adverse events generally occurred in greater proportions of patients aged ≥65 versus <65 years. There was generally a higher rate of premature trial product discontinuation because of adverse events in the older age group. These results indicate that oral semaglutide is efficacious in Japanese patients irrespective of age.</snippet>
<snippet id="35355921">Title: Efficacy and safety of novel twincretin tirzepatide a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist in the management of type-2 diabetes: A Cochrane meta-analysis.
Authors: Dutta, Deep, Surana, Vineet, Singla, Rajiv et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Indian journal of endocrinology and metabolism
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Till date, there is no Cochrane meta-analysis available which has analyzed efficacy and safety of tirzepatide in type-2 diabetes. This meta-analysis was undertaken to address this knowledge gap.
METHODS
Electronic databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving people with diabetes receiving tirzepatide compared to a placebo/active comparator. Primary outcome was to evaluate changes in HbA1c. Secondary outcomes were to evaluate alterations in blood-glucose, glycemic targets, weight, lipids, and adverse events.
RESULTS
From 34 articles initially screened, data from six RCTs involving 3484 patients were analyzed. Over 12-52 weeks, individuals receiving tirzepatide had significantly greater lowering of HbA1c [mean difference (MD) = -0.75% (95% confidence interval (CI): -1.05 to -0.45); P < 0.01; I  2 = 100%], fasting glucose [MD = -0.75 mmol/L (95% CI: -1.05 to- -0.45); P < 0.01; I  2 = 100%], 2-h post-prandial-glucose [MD = -0.87 mmol/L (95% CI: -1.12 to -0.61); P < 0.01; I  2 = 99%], weight [MD = -8.63 kg (95% CI: -12.89 to -4.36); P < 0.01; I  2 = 100%], body mass index [MD = -1.80 kg/m 2 (95% CI: -2.39 to -1.21); P < 0.01; I  2 = 99%], and waist circumference [MD = -4.43 cm (95% CI: -5.31 to -3.55); P < 0.01; I  2 = 95%] as compared to dulaglutide, semaglutide, degludec, or glargine. Patients receiving tirzepatide had higher odds of achieving HbA1c <6.5% compared to active controls [odds ratio (OR) = 4.39 (95% CI: 2.44-7.92); P < 0.01; I  2 = 90%]. Tirzepatide use had significantly higher odds of weight loss >5% [OR = 19.18 (95% CI: 2.34-157.17); P < 0.01; I  2 = 99%], >10% [OR = 21.40 (95% CI: 2.36-193.94); P < 0.01; I  2 = 98%], and >15% [OR = 32.84 (95% CI: 2.27-474.33); P = 0.01; I  2 = 96%] compared to active-control group. Treatment-emergent adverse events [risk ratio (RR) = 1.43 (95% CI: 1.14-1.80); P < 0.01; I  2 = 40%] and severe adverse events [RR = 1.00 (95% CI: 0.64-1.57); P = 1.00; I  2 = 49%] were not different. High data heterogeneity and the presence of publication bias limits the grading of current data from "moderate to low."
CONCLUSION
Tirzepatide has impressive glycemic efficacy and weight-loss data over 1-year clinical use. The need for higher grade, long-term efficacy, and safety data remains.</snippet>

# Summary

- Over at least 52 weeks in type 2 diabetes, semaglutide (0.5–1.0 mg once-weekly) demonstrates larger mean HbA1c reductions and greater body weight losses than dulaglutide (0.75–4.5 mg once-weekly), based on direct trial-derived modeling and network meta-analysis, with the largest differences favoring semaglutide in head-to-head comparisons at commonly used doses (0.5 mg semaglutide vs 0.75 mg dulaglutide). <cite id="34697882">Model-based simulations using SUSTAIN (semaglutide) and AWARD-11 (dulaglutide) data showed that at 52 weeks, switching from semaglutide 0.5 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 mg yielded additional HbA1c reductions of 0.19% and weight reductions of 1.40 kg, while switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 4.5 mg maintained HbA1c with an additional 0.57 kg weight loss</cite> <cite id="29574633">A network meta-analysis in Japanese T2D patients found semaglutide 0.5 mg once-weekly reduced HbA1c by 0.61% (12.3 mmol/mol) and weight by 1.45 kg compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg once-weekly at 52–56 weeks, with no significant difference in hypoglycemia or HbA1c <7% achievement</cite> <cite id="29932006">A broader review of semaglutide reported HbA1c reductions of 1.1–2.2% across multiple trials and weight losses of 1.4–6.5 kg, and showed greater efficacy than comparators including dulaglutide</cite>.

- In phase 3 settings, semaglutide's clinically meaningful HbA1c and weight effects are sustained over ≥52 weeks, with additional weight reduction advantages versus dulaglutide at higher dulaglutide doses (3–4.5 mg) in switching models, though glycemic control may be preserved when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 mg. <cite id="34697882">Simulations over 52 weeks indicated that higher-dose dulaglutide (4.5 mg) could modestly enhance weight loss after switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg while maintaining HbA1c, whereas lower-dose dulaglutide (3.0 mg) improved both HbA1c and weight compared with continued semaglutide 0.5 mg</cite>.

# HbA1c Reduction

- Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW vs dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW: Mean HbA1c reduction −0.61% (12.3 mmol/mol) favoring semaglutide at 52–56 weeks. <cite id="29574633">Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW reduced HbA1c by 0.61% compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW in a network meta-analysis of trials lasting 52–56 weeks</cite>.

- Across semaglutide trials, HbA1c reductions range from approximately 1.1% to 2.2% over multi-year durations, exceeding dulaglutide's effects in indirect comparisons and reviews. <cite id="29932006">Semaglutide achieved HbA1c reductions of 1.1–2.2% across studies 30–104 weeks, outperforming comparators including dulaglutide</cite>.

- Switching analyses suggest dulaglutide 3.0 mg can add small HbA1c improvements versus continuing semaglutide 0.5 mg, but overall the magnitude is modest and semaglutide's baseline effect is larger. <cite id="34697882">After 26 weeks of semaglutide 0.5 mg (−1.55% HbA1c), switching to dulaglutide 3.0 mg added an additional −0.19% at 52 weeks; after 26 weeks of semaglutide 1.0 mg (−1.84% HbA1c), switching to dulaglutide 4.5 mg maintained HbA1c</cite>.

# Body Weight

- Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW vs dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW: Mean weight loss −3.44 kg (semaglutide 0.5 mg over 26 weeks) and −1.45 kg (dulaglutide 0.75 mg), with larger cumulative losses favoring semaglutide in indirect evidence. <cite id="34697882">At 26 weeks, semaglutide 0.5 mg predicted −3.44 kg weight loss versus dulaglutide 0.75 mg −1.45 kg at 52 weeks in Japanese data synthesis</cite> <cite id="29574633">Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW reduced weight by 1.45 kg compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW at 52–56 weeks</cite>.

- Over ≥52 weeks, semaglutide produces clinically meaningful weight losses (approximately −4.0 to −5.0 kg at 1.0 mg) that are generally greater than dulaglutide's effects, with higher-dose dulaglutide (4.5 mg) adding at most ~0.57 kg further loss when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg. <cite id="34697882">At 26 weeks, semaglutide 1.0 mg predicted −4.96 kg weight loss; switching to dulaglutide 4.5 mg at 52 weeks added only ~0.57 kg further loss, indicating semaglutide's superior sustained weight effect</cite> <cite id="29932006">Semaglutide trials reported weight reductions of 1.4–6.5 kg across 30–104 weeks, with dulaglutide comparators showing smaller effects</cite>.

# Context and Limitations

- Direct head-to-head phase III trials between semaglutide and dulaglutide are limited; many comparative estimates come from network meta-analyses and exposure–response modeling. <cite id="29574633">The absence of head-to-head trials in specific populations led to network meta-analytic comparisons between semaglutide 0.5 mg and dulaglutide 0.75 mg</cite> <cite id="34697882">Model-based simulations integrated semaglutide SUSTAIN trials and dulaglutide AWARD-11 to project 52-week outcomes after switching</cite>.

- Switching models may not reflect optimal-label dosing or continued treatment in the same patient; thus, effect sizes can differ from within-treatment comparisons. <cite id="34697882">Simulations assumed structured titration schedules and dose escalations that may not mirror real-world adherence or labeling</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In phase III-era evidence over ≥52 weeks, semaglutide provides greater HbA1c reductions (≈1.5–2.2% across trials; ≈0.61% vs 0.75 mg dulaglutide in indirect comparisons) and larger body weight losses (≈3–5 kg at standard doses; ≈1.45 kg vs 0.75 mg dulaglutide in indirect comparisons) than dulaglutide, with higher-dose dulaglutide (3–4.5 mg) adding at most modest additional weight loss and preserving glycemia when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg. <cite id="29932006">Semaglutide's HbA1c and weight effects exceed dulaglutide comparators across long-duration trials</cite> <cite id="29574633">Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW outperformed dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW for HbA1c and weight at 52–56 weeks</cite> <cite id="34697882">Switching analyses indicate dulaglutide 3.0–4.5 mg can add small HbA1c and weight changes relative to continued semaglutide</cite>.

data.title: Semaglutide: The Newest Once-Weekly GLP-1 RA for Type 2 Diabetes.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To review efficacy and safety of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) semaglutide for type 2 diabetes (T2D).
DATA SOURCES
A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and EMBASE using the term semaglutide was completed through April 2018. A search of clinicaltrials.gov was also conducted.
STUDY SELECTION AND DATA EXTRACTION
English-language studies assessing the efficacy and/or safety of semaglutide were evaluated.
DATA SYNTHESIS
Semaglutide is a newly approved GLP-1 RA for the treatment of T2D. Administered once weekly at a dose of 0.5 or 1 mg, it has been compared with placebo, sitagliptin, insulin glargine, a combination of oral antidiabetic therapies, and 2 GLP-1 RAs, exenatide ER and dulaglutide, and demonstrated greater efficacy compared with these therapies. Published data from studies ranging from 30 to 104 weeks duration demonstrate efficacy with decreases in hemoglobin A1C (A1C) ranging from 1.1% to 2.2%. Studies show reductions in weight from 1.4 to 6.5 kg. Semaglutide demonstrated a reduction in the composite outcome of cardiovascular (CV) death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke compared with placebo in patients at high risk of CV events (hazard ratio = 0.74; P = 0.02). Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea as seen with other GLP-1 RAs. Relevance to Patient Care and Clinical Practice: Semaglutide represents an attractive GLP-1 RA considering its A1C and weight reduction. It provides patient convenience and high patient satisfaction.
CONCLUSIONS
Semaglutide is an appealing option for the treatment of T2D as a once-weekly GLP-1 RA with established glycemic, CV, and weight benefits.

data.title: A model-based simulation of glycaemic control and body weight when switching from semaglutide to 3.0- and 4.5-mg doses of once-weekly dulaglutide.
data.abstract:
AIM
To evaluate HbA1c and body weight changes when semaglutide 0.5- or 1.0-mg once-weekly (QW) is switched to dulaglutide 3.0- or 4.5-mg QW via exposure-response modelling.
METHODS
HbA1c and body weight time-course models were developed and validated with data from the SUSTAIN 1 to 10 trials for semaglutide and the AWARD-11 trial for dulaglutide. Simulations were conducted for HbA1c and body weight over 52 weeks. In the initial 26 weeks, semaglutide was initiated at 0.25-mg and titrated to 0.5- or 1.0-mg QW via 4-weekly stepwise titration, followed by 26 weeks of dulaglutide initiated at 0.75- or 1.5-mg QW and escalated to 3.0- or 4.5-mg QW via 4-weekly stepwise titration.
RESULTS
At 26 weeks, model-predicted mean changes from baseline in HbA1c and weight for semaglutide 0.5 mg were up to -1.55% and -3.44 kg, respectively. After switching to dulaglutide 3.0 mg, further reductions were 0.19% and 1.40 kg, respectively, at 52 weeks. Predicted mean HbA1c and weight changes for semaglutide 1.0 mg at 26 weeks were -1.84% and -4.96 kg, respectively; after switching to dulaglutide 4.5 mg, HbA1c was maintained with additional weight reduction of up to 0.57 kg at 52 weeks. Glycaemic control was preserved when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 mg.
CONCLUSION
Switching from semaglutide 0.5 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 or 4.5 mg with dose escalation potentially yields additional HbA1c and weight reductions; switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 4.5 mg may enhance weight loss.

data.title: A Network Meta-Analysis Comparing Semaglutide Once-Weekly with Other GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Japanese Patients with Type 2 Diabetes.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Semaglutide once-weekly (QW) is a novel glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) analogue administered at a 0.5 or 1.0 mg dose. In the absence of head-to-head trials between semaglutide QW and other GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) in a Japanese population, a network meta-analysis (NMA) was performed. The objective was to assess the relative efficacy and safety of semaglutide QW vs GLP-1 RAs in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM), with a specific focus on the comparison between semaglutide 0.5 mg QW and dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW.
METHODS
A systematic review (SR) and supplementary Japanese searches were conducted to identify trials of GLP-1 RAs in Japanese patients on diet and exercise, who have previously received 0-1 oral antidiabetic drugs (OADs). Data at 52-56 weeks were extracted for the following outcomes (feasible for analysis in an NMA): glycated hemoglobin (HbA 1c ), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), weight, systolic blood pressure (SBP), and overall hypoglycemia. The data were synthesized using an NMA and a Bayesian framework.
RESULTS
Four trials, identified from the SR and Japanese-specific searches, were relevant for inclusion in the NMA. When compared to dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW, semaglutide 0.5 mg QW was shown to provide significant reductions in HbA 1c [- 0.61% (12.3 mmol/mol)], weight (- 1.45 kg), SBP (- 5.03 mmHg), and FPG (- 1.26 mmol/L). No significant differences in the proportion of patients achieving a HbA 1c level < 7% (53 mmol/mol) or the risk of overall hypoglycemia were observed between semaglutide 0.5 mg QW and dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW.
CONCLUSION
Overall, semaglutide 0.5 mg QW was associated with significant reductions from baseline in HbA 1c , weight, SBP, and FPG compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW in Japanese patients with T2DM. These data may provide valuable evidence for clinical decision-making, cost-effectiveness analyses, and health technology appraisal (HTA) requirements.
FUNDING
Novo Nordisk Pharma Ltd.

data.title: Efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide by baseline age in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes: A subgroup analysis of the PIONEER 9 and 10 Japan trials.
data.abstract: A post-hoc exploratory analysis of the PIONEER 9 and 10 trials evaluated the effect of baseline age (<65 and ≥65 years) on the efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes. In PIONEER 9 and 10, patients were randomized to once-daily oral semaglutide (3, 7 or 14 mg) or a comparator (placebo or once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide 0.9 mg [PIONEER 9]; once-weekly subcutaneous dulaglutide 0.75 mg [PIONEER 10]) for 52 weeks, with 5 weeks' follow-up. In total, 701 patients were included (PIONEER 9: N = 243; PIONEER 10: N = 458). Glycaemic efficacy of oral semaglutide was similar in Japanese patients aged <65 years compared with those ≥65 years, and there did not appear to be a clear pattern between age subgroup and body weight changes. Across treatment arms, adverse events generally occurred in greater proportions of patients aged ≥65 versus <65 years. There was generally a higher rate of premature trial product discontinuation because of adverse events in the older age group. These results indicate that oral semaglutide is efficacious in Japanese patients irrespective of age.

data.title: Efficacy and safety of novel twincretin tirzepatide a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist in the management of type-2 diabetes: A Cochrane meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Till date, there is no Cochrane meta-analysis available which has analyzed efficacy and safety of tirzepatide in type-2 diabetes. This meta-analysis was undertaken to address this knowledge gap.
METHODS
Electronic databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving people with diabetes receiving tirzepatide compared to a placebo/active comparator. Primary outcome was to evaluate changes in HbA1c. Secondary outcomes were to evaluate alterations in blood-glucose, glycemic targets, weight, lipids, and adverse events.
RESULTS
From 34 articles initially screened, data from six RCTs involving 3484 patients were analyzed. Over 12-52 weeks, individuals receiving tirzepatide had significantly greater lowering of HbA1c [mean difference (MD) = -0.75% (95% confidence interval (CI): -1.05 to -0.45); P < 0.01; I  2 = 100%], fasting glucose [MD = -0.75 mmol/L (95% CI: -1.05 to- -0.45); P < 0.01; I  2 = 100%], 2-h post-prandial-glucose [MD = -0.87 mmol/L (95% CI: -1.12 to -0.61); P < 0.01; I  2 = 99%], weight [MD = -8.63 kg (95% CI: -12.89 to -4.36); P < 0.01; I  2 = 100%], body mass index [MD = -1.80 kg/m 2 (95% CI: -2.39 to -1.21); P < 0.01; I  2 = 99%], and waist circumference [MD = -4.43 cm (95% CI: -5.31 to -3.55); P < 0.01; I  2 = 95%] as compared to dulaglutide, semaglutide, degludec, or glargine. Patients receiving tirzepatide had higher odds of achieving HbA1c <6.5% compared to active controls [odds ratio (OR) = 4.39 (95% CI: 2.44-7.92); P < 0.01; I  2 = 90%]. Tirzepatide use had significantly higher odds of weight loss >5% [OR = 19.18 (95% CI: 2.34-157.17); P < 0.01; I  2 = 99%], >10% [OR = 21.40 (95% CI: 2.36-193.94); P < 0.01; I  2 = 98%], and >15% [OR = 32.84 (95% CI: 2.27-474.33); P = 0.01; I  2 = 96%] compared to active-control group. Treatment-emergent adverse events [risk ratio (RR) = 1.43 (95% CI: 1.14-1.80); P < 0.01; I  2 = 40%] and severe adverse events [RR = 1.00 (95% CI: 0.64-1.57); P = 1.00; I  2 = 49%] were not different. High data heterogeneity and the presence of publication bias limits the grading of current data from "moderate to low."
CONCLUSION
Tirzepatide has impressive glycemic efficacy and weight-loss data over 1-year clinical use. The need for higher grade, long-term efficacy, and safety data remains.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

- Over at least 52 weeks in type 2 diabetes, semaglutide (0.5–1.0 mg once-weekly) demonstrates larger mean HbA1c reductions and greater body weight losses than dulaglutide (0.75–4.5 mg once-weekly), based on direct trial-derived modeling and network meta-analysis, with the largest differences favoring semaglutide in head-to-head comparisons at commonly used doses (0.5 mg semaglutide vs 0.75 mg dulaglutide). <cite id="34697882">Model-based simulations using SUSTAIN (semaglutide) and AWARD-11 (dulaglutide) data showed that at 52 weeks, switching from semaglutide 0.5 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 mg yielded additional HbA1c reductions of 0.19% and weight reductions of 1.40 kg, while switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 4.5 mg maintained HbA1c with an additional 0.57 kg weight loss</cite> <cite id="29574633">A network meta-analysis in Japanese T2D patients found semaglutide 0.5 mg once-weekly reduced HbA1c by 0.61% (12.3 mmol/mol) and weight by 1.45 kg compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg once-weekly at 52–56 weeks, with no significant difference in hypoglycemia or HbA1c <7% achievement</cite> <cite id="29932006">A broader review of semaglutide reported HbA1c reductions of 1.1–2.2% across multiple trials and weight losses of 1.4–6.5 kg, and showed greater efficacy than comparators including dulaglutide</cite>.

- In phase 3 settings, semaglutide's clinically meaningful HbA1c and weight effects are sustained over ≥52 weeks, with additional weight reduction advantages versus dulaglutide at higher dulaglutide doses (3–4.5 mg) in switching models, though glycemic control may be preserved when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg to dulaglutide 3.0 mg. <cite id="34697882">Simulations over 52 weeks indicated that higher-dose dulaglutide (4.5 mg) could modestly enhance weight loss after switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg while maintaining HbA1c, whereas lower-dose dulaglutide (3.0 mg) improved both HbA1c and weight compared with continued semaglutide 0.5 mg</cite>.

# HbA1c Reduction

- Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW vs dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW: Mean HbA1c reduction −0.61% (12.3 mmol/mol) favoring semaglutide at 52–56 weeks. <cite id="29574633">Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW reduced HbA1c by 0.61% compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW in a network meta-analysis of trials lasting 52–56 weeks</cite>.

- Across semaglutide trials, HbA1c reductions range from approximately 1.1% to 2.2% over multi-year durations, exceeding dulaglutide's effects in indirect comparisons and reviews. <cite id="29932006">Semaglutide achieved HbA1c reductions of 1.1–2.2% across studies 30–104 weeks, outperforming comparators including dulaglutide</cite>.

- Switching analyses suggest dulaglutide 3.0 mg can add small HbA1c improvements versus continuing semaglutide 0.5 mg, but overall the magnitude is modest and semaglutide's baseline effect is larger. <cite id="34697882">After 26 weeks of semaglutide 0.5 mg (−1.55% HbA1c), switching to dulaglutide 3.0 mg added an additional −0.19% at 52 weeks; after 26 weeks of semaglutide 1.0 mg (−1.84% HbA1c), switching to dulaglutide 4.5 mg maintained HbA1c</cite>.

# Body Weight

- Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW vs dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW: Mean weight loss −3.44 kg (semaglutide 0.5 mg over 26 weeks) and −1.45 kg (dulaglutide 0.75 mg), with larger cumulative losses favoring semaglutide in indirect evidence. <cite id="34697882">At 26 weeks, semaglutide 0.5 mg predicted −3.44 kg weight loss versus dulaglutide 0.75 mg −1.45 kg at 52 weeks in Japanese data synthesis</cite> <cite id="29574633">Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW reduced weight by 1.45 kg compared with dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW at 52–56 weeks</cite>.

- Over ≥52 weeks, semaglutide produces clinically meaningful weight losses (approximately −4.0 to −5.0 kg at 1.0 mg) that are generally greater than dulaglutide's effects, with higher-dose dulaglutide (4.5 mg) adding at most ~0.57 kg further loss when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg. <cite id="34697882">At 26 weeks, semaglutide 1.0 mg predicted −4.96 kg weight loss; switching to dulaglutide 4.5 mg at 52 weeks added only ~0.57 kg further loss, indicating semaglutide's superior sustained weight effect</cite> <cite id="29932006">Semaglutide trials reported weight reductions of 1.4–6.5 kg across 30–104 weeks, with dulaglutide comparators showing smaller effects</cite>.

# Context and Limitations

- Direct head-to-head phase III trials between semaglutide and dulaglutide are limited; many comparative estimates come from network meta-analyses and exposure–response modeling. <cite id="29574633">The absence of head-to-head trials in specific populations led to network meta-analytic comparisons between semaglutide 0.5 mg and dulaglutide 0.75 mg</cite> <cite id="34697882">Model-based simulations integrated semaglutide SUSTAIN trials and dulaglutide AWARD-11 to project 52-week outcomes after switching</cite>.

- Switching models may not reflect optimal-label dosing or continued treatment in the same patient; thus, effect sizes can differ from within-treatment comparisons. <cite id="34697882">Simulations assumed structured titration schedules and dose escalations that may not mirror real-world adherence or labeling</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In phase III-era evidence over ≥52 weeks, semaglutide provides greater HbA1c reductions (≈1.5–2.2% across trials; ≈0.61% vs 0.75 mg dulaglutide in indirect comparisons) and larger body weight losses (≈3–5 kg at standard doses; ≈1.45 kg vs 0.75 mg dulaglutide in indirect comparisons) than dulaglutide, with higher-dose dulaglutide (3–4.5 mg) adding at most modest additional weight loss and preserving glycemia when switching from semaglutide 1.0 mg. <cite id="29932006">Semaglutide's HbA1c and weight effects exceed dulaglutide comparators across long-duration trials</cite> <cite id="29574633">Semaglutide 0.5 mg QW outperformed dulaglutide 0.75 mg QW for HbA1c and weight at 52–56 weeks</cite> <cite id="34697882">Switching analyses indicate dulaglutide 3.0–4.5 mg can add small HbA1c and weight changes relative to continued semaglutide</cite>.
